status: two chapters revised · comparison hall restored
summary: Four local editorial changes preserve the investigative voice. The missing Rule 90/pyramid hall is now restored between Soft Rules and Edge of Chaos, with both works primary. Two further text changes invite the controls and seed comparison now available there.

items.title: Six chapters already carry the investigation
items.description: Preserve the first five chapters and Edge of Chaos. Their questions arise from ordered neighbours, lingering states, a history underfoot, a travelling pattern, lost support and a difference altered by storage. Keep every code block and artifact marker in this sequence.

items.title: CA SoftRules · A room can wear a field
items.description: Let the same texture become an encounter at another scale, with room for desire and another possible use. Keep the fixed-floor fact here and the additional implementation limits in a note.
items.before: Now walk between the two curved displays. COAT removes their colour surfaces while the table fields continue. Bring them back. Nothing has moved from the table into the architecture: each pair uses the same texture. The fixed museum floor carries you through both versions. The room can wear this process, and later another body could wear it, but a material assignment has not supplied sensation, growth or agency.
items.after:
Now walk between the two curved displays. Find a patch on a wall, then look for it on the table. Each pair shares the same texture. At the desk you could take in the small field; here you turn within its enlarged image.

Press COAT. The colour surfaces disappear while the table fields continue. Bring them back. The fixed museum floor carries you through both views.[^ca-soft-coating] The field has become something the room can wear. Perhaps you would keep it here, or want it closer, as a lining against a body. What would you change for that other use?

items.title: CA SoftRules · Carry an unfinished resemblance forward
items.description: Carry the question from Soft Rules into the local-rule/pyramid comparison. That next hall has now been restored in the museum as well as the book order.
items.before: The local study holds after 2,400 updates. The museum goes on. Carry the matched beginning and the visible clock into the next hall: when a small intervention changes an outcome, how will we tell what actually changed?
items.after: The local study holds after 2,400 updates. The museum goes on. We have watched a field change and a room wear its image. Carry a question from those surfaces: could a similar form have another way of becoming?

items.title: CA AgentsCircuits · Give the gap a neighbour to remember
items.description: Keep the review's careful comparison of one relation, including where it fails. Replace assessment-like instructions with a small act of looking and carrying something to the second work.
items.before: Before leaving the rule display, choose one gap whose position you could describe to someone else. Describe the occupied cells around it as well as the empty region itself. A pattern can appear similar because its holes correspond, because its filled parts correspond, or because its outline does. Those are different comparisons. Carry that description to the pyramid and test only the relation you chose first. If it fails, locate the precise mismatch before choosing another relation; otherwise resemblance can become a moving target that never risks being wrong.
items.after: Choose one triangular gap in the rule display. Keep a few occupied cells around it in mind, so there is more to recognise than the outline. Carry that small arrangement to the pyramid. Where would it fit? If one part refuses the match, stay with that part before choosing a different resemblance. We have found something the shared appearance did not tell us.

items.title: CA AgentsCircuits · Let recognition invite another experiment
items.description: Keep the different procedures and the proposed seed experiment. Move the warning about computing claims into a note, and correct the transition to the existing paired-difference study rather than reintroducing graded states.
items.before:
Both encounters produce organised patterns, but neither appearance alone proves the presence of an agent, a circuit or a general-purpose computer. Those claims require additional structure: states that can represent something, operations that transform them, and a way of checking the result.

A useful variation would keep the pyramid fixed while trying several different seeds in Rule 90. Some seeds preserve familiar triangular relations; others overlap them. The comparison would expose how much the resemblance depends on the starting condition.

<!-- @ -->

Next, the sequence asks what happens when a local update admits graded states and disturbance. Keep asking whether a name describes an observed relation or simply encourages you to see one.
items.after:
The row's next state and the pyramid's smaller copies can lead the eye towards a related form. The pleasure of recognising it gives us a reason to compare their making. A name for the resemblance can accompany that inquiry without finishing it.[^ca-resemblance]

A useful variation would keep the pyramid fixed while trying several different seeds in Rule 90. Some seeds preserve familiar triangular relations; others overlap them. The comparison would expose how much the resemblance depends on the starting condition.

<!-- @ -->

We will return to the pyramid's way of making in Fractals. First, two almost matching volumes will let us follow one changed value through the same procedure. We have asked how similar appearances can be made differently. What happens when we keep the making the same and alter one small part of the beginning?

items.title: The comparison has its room again
items.description: Rule 90 near the entrance; the recursive pyramid farther on; a continuous floor between them and room to walk around the volume. Both existing works remain primary. The desk has its own legs, with its controls about 1.08 m above the floor. All eight CA halls now appear in the declared museum order.

items.title: Build the history at your own pace
items.description: The prose now invites an operation supported by the restored desk.
items.before: Set the rule explorer to Rule 90 and reset its central seed. Follow the triangular gaps that develop between occupied cells. Choose a larger triangle and look for smaller ones arranged within its boundary. Let the rule continue until you can compare more than one scale.
items.after: Set the rule explorer to Rule 90 and reset its central seed. Press STEP a few times. Follow the triangular gaps that develop between occupied cells. Choose a larger triangle and look for smaller ones arranged within its boundary. Add another row when you need more to compare.

items.title: From a future variation to a present encounter
items.description: The prose now invites an operation supported by the restored desk.
items.before: A useful variation would keep the pyramid fixed while trying several different seeds in Rule 90. Some seeds preserve familiar triangular relations; others overlap them. The comparison would expose how much the resemblance depends on the starting condition.
items.after: Keep the pyramid fixed and press SEED at the desk. Two adjacent cells now begin the history. Build a few rows again. Where do the familiar triangular relations return, and where do they overlap? Press SEED once more to return to the single cell. How much of the resemblance belonged to the rule, and how much to the beginning we gave it?
